title: Chirality-induced spin selectivity as a nonequilibrium effect: a unified test of competing mechanisms
abstract: For two decades, the origin of Chirality-Induced Spin Selectivity (CISS), the spin polarization of electrons by nonmagnetic chiral systems without magnetic fields, has remained unsettled. Here, we establish a single exact rule defining the fundamental conditions for the effect: in nonmagnetic, time-reversal-invariant conductors, all measurable CISS signals are time-reversal odd and vanish near equilibrium, proving that structural chirality alone is insufficient. By evaluating leading theoretical mechanisms across four levels of nonequilibrium transport, from coherent classical driving to fully non-Markovian quantum baths, we verify this selection rule to machine precision. We show that coherent chiral vibrations generate substantial collinear polarization (up to 10 percent across 0.5-6 THz) that reverses with handedness, whereas incoherent vibrations yield under 1 percent, and non-Markovian bath memory further suppresses the signal. The chiral geometry first makes the electronic motion chiral by accumulating orbital angular momentum; spin-orbit coupling (SOC) then converts that into spin. CISS therefore acts as both a spin polarizer and a spin filter, the latter an order of magnitude weaker. The polarization grows with molecular length and then saturates, matching trends reported for DNA and peptides. Reversing the drive converts decaying spin into a handedness-locked charge-current pulse (inverse-CISS). We find that once the system is driven, the polarization magnitude scales with an effective spin-orbit coupling: making heavy atoms and curved light-atom backbones indistinguishable at equivalent effective SOC. This enables us to chart how geometry, driving field, and length separate those routes.
summary: This paper provides a unified theoretical framework to understand Chirality-Induced Spin Selectivity (CISS), proving that the effect requires breaking both parity and time-reversal symmetry. By analyzing various non-equilibrium transport regimes, the authors demonstrate that coherent chiral vibrations are essential for generating measurable spin polarization, providing a crucial diagnostic tool for future spintronic materials.
main_problem: The fundamental origin of Chirality-Induced Spin Selectivity (CISS)—the spin polarization of electrons by nonmagnetic chiral systems without external magnetic fields—remains theoretically unsettled.
main_result: The authors establish a strict selection rule: measurable CISS signals must be time-reversal odd and vanish near equilibrium, proving structural chirality alone is insufficient. They show that coherent chiral vibrations are necessary to generate substantial, handedness-reversing spin polarization.
method: The study evaluates leading theoretical mechanisms across four levels of non-equilibrium transport, ranging from coherent classical driving to fully non-Markovian quantum baths, using advanced Green's function techniques.
model_or_system: The analysis employs a minimal single-orbital tight-binding Hamiltonian on a helix, later extended to a more realistic p-orbital model to separate orbital and spin chirality. The system is driven by both coherent and incoherent phonon baths.
key_observables: Spin polarization ($P_z$), polarization magnitude (up to 10% for coherent drive), and the reversal of polarization with handedness (Inverse-CISS).
important_parameters: The polarization scales with an effective spin-orbit coupling (SOC), allowing comparison between heavy atoms and curved light-atom backbones.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on modeling the system's response to various phonon coupling mechanisms and assumes the validity of the four levels of non-equilibrium transport theory.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates that equilibrium yields zero polarization due to time-reversal symmetry, while a chiral drive breaks this symmetry, generating spin polarization via the conversion of orbital angular momentum to spin via SOC.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the CISS effect by first establishing the necessary symmetry constraints, then modeling the system using minimal and p-orbital Hamiltonians, and finally testing various non-equilibrium transport regimes (coherent vs. incoherent driving) to pinpoint the required physical mechanism.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses non-equilibrium spin transport in mesoscopic chiral systems, which is highly relevant to understanding spin-orbit coupling effects in molecular electronics and spintronics, bridging concepts from quantum optics and condensed matter theory.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Concept. (a) In equilibrium a chiral conductor between two nonmagnetic leads carries no spin polarization: time- reversal symmetry forces Pz = 0, and equal up- and down-spin flows cancel. (b) A chiral drive (a coherent vibration, a bias, or a magnetic contact) breaks time-reversal symmetry and the transmitted current becomes spin polarized, Pz ̸= 0. Structural chirality produces an orbital moment Lz, which spin-orbit coupling converts into spin Sz.

FIG. 2. Single-orbital model. (a) Intrinsic polarization Pz versus drive frequency Ω(THz scale; the calculation uses Ω/t) for right- and left-handed helices (N = 200) and a straight control, from the coherent Floquet drive [Eq. (3)]. (b) Pz versus chain length. (c) Magnetoresistance PMR versus normalized electron-phonon coupling for the same vibration treated three ways (Table I): weak thermal phonon (A, SCBA), the same with finite phonon spectral linewidth η (B, SCBA), and the coherent drive (C, Floquet).

FIG. 3. Single-orbital model, coherent Floquet drive. Parameter dependence of Pz, averaged over disorder and energy. Left: SOC versus Fermi level. Middle: drive strength versus disorder. Right: SOC versus temperature at fixed drive. The straight control is unpolarized in every panel.

FIG. 4. Temperature (single-orbital model). Left: coherent Floquet drive, |Pz(T)| for several vibration frequencies, with the drive scaled by the thermal factor (solid) and held fixed (dashed). Right: a frozen, thermally distorted static lattice (elastic), |Pz(T)|.
FIG. 5. Single-orbital model, GKBA, N = 12. Steady spin accumulation Pz versus vibration memory time τc, at weak and at strong coupling.
